analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling and steers royalty money to infrastructure.
analysis.headline: The bill had 7 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never received a committee markup or a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened new areas of federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling, including areas near Florida that are currently under a drilling moratorium. It would have declared a stalled offshore leasing program legally approved and its environmental review finished, shortened and narrowed court challenges to drilling decisions, and let the president waive legal requirements for projects it deems nationally important. To win support, it would have sent a share of drilling royalties to coastal states and routed 60% of new royalties, plus proceeds from swapping crude in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, into a fund for roads, transit, and water projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: new lease sales across every outer Continental Shelf planning area with commercial interest, the reopening of moratorium areas in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, a pre-approved leasing program with a deemed-final environmental statement, expedited court review, and a presidential waiver power. Construction firms gain if the new royalty-funded Infrastructure Renewal Reserve finances highway, transit, and water work. Coastal producing states would receive 30% of royalties from new leases, usable for education, transportation, coastal restoration, and energy programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, construction firms, and coastal states

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to hold a lease sale in every outer Continental Shelf planning area with commercial interest, starting within 30 days of enactment, and repeals the Gulf of Mexico moratoria near Florida, including a final leasing plan for the Eastern Gulf.
Declares the stalled 2010-2015 offshore leasing program approved as final and its environmental impact statement complete, so leasing can proceed without finishing the normal review process.

Creates an Infrastructure Renewal Reserve funded by 60% of royalties from new leases plus 90% of net proceeds from exchanging light for heavy crude in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, to pay for federal highway, public transportation, and Army Corps water construction projects.
Pays 30% of royalties from new leases to producing coastal states, which may spend it on education, transportation, coastal restoration, energy infrastructure, renewable energy, and efficiency.
Sends 10% of new-lease royalties to the Treasury general fund solely for paying down the national debt.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities and ocean users bear new drilling risk off the Atlantic and Florida coasts, with environmental safeguards reduced: the leasing program is approved by statute with no completed environmental review, challenges are confined to the D.C. Circuit with a 30-day filing window, losing challengers must pay the other side's legal fees, administrative findings are presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence, and the president can waive any legal requirement. The Treasury's share of new royalties is cut to 10% once 30% goes to states and 60% to the infrastructure fund, and the infrastructure money only arrives if companies actually bid on leases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities, ocean users, and federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill would have deemed the 2010-2015 leasing program approved and its environmental impact statement final by statute, bypassing the ordinary process for completing and reviewing that analysis before opening new waters to drilling.

It would have confined all challenges to federal oil and gas leasing decisions to the D.C. Circuit, barred petitions filed more than 30 days after the action, required losing challengers to pay the winners' legal fees, presumed administrative findings correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence, and let the president waive any legal requirement for a project he deems in the national interest.
It would have repealed the moratorium on leasing east of the Military Mission Line in the Gulf and in areas within 100-125 miles of the Florida coast, expanding drilling near Florida's coasts.

The infrastructure funding is not guaranteed: it depends on companies bidding for leases in waters where demand is uncertain, and the bill also bans offshore wind and other inventory work from restricting any leasing or drilling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The infrastructure and state revenue provisions are real and would have directed money to roads, transit, and water systems, and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve swap follows a GAO recommendation to hold crude refiners can actually use. But the funding stream is speculative — it exists only if drilling companies bid on newly opened waters — and the core of the bill is a large expansion of offshore drilling that achieves its public benefits by dismantling the environmental review and court-access safeguards that normally apply to exactly this kind of high-risk activity. An honest supporter would concede that the bill buys infrastructure with coastal spill risk and weaker legal recourse, and buys it only if the leasing gamble pays off.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees and four subcommittees in early 2013, never received a markup or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Murphy introduced the bill on February 15, 2013, and it was referred to the Natural Resources, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Rules, Budget, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees.

It was then sent to subcommittees on Energy and Power, Highways and Transit, Water Resources and Environment, Railroads Pipelines and Hazardous Materials, Energy and Mineral Resources, and Regulatory Reform Commercial and Antitrust Law, with the last referral on April 8, 2013.
No further action is recorded: no committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill had 7 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democratic cosponsor.

Had it passed, it would have opened new offshore areas including near Florida to leasing, deemed the 2010-2015 leasing program and its environmental statement approved, and created a royalty-funded infrastructure reserve.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new law. The status quo held: drilling moratoria near Florida stayed in place, the stalled leasing program was not statutorily approved, and coastal waters were not opened for new oil and gas leasing during the Congress. The oil and gas industry kept its existing access but did not win the new areas; coastal states did not receive the promised 30% royalty share, and the infrastructure fund was never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities; moratoria stayed in place

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill; it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on March 1, 2013 and never marked up or reported.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 members attached to the bill (the sponsor plus 7 cosponsors) were Republicans, but the bill never reached a committee or floor vote, so no recorded vote shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill hands the industry new lease sales across the outer Continental Shelf, reopens moratorium areas in the eastern Gulf, pre-approves the leasing program and its environmental statement by statute, speeds and narrows court challenges, and adds a presidential waiver power. Its gain comes from opening public waters and weakening the review and litigation safeguards that protect coastal residents, who bear the spill and pollution risk.

industries.industry: Road, transit, and water infrastructure construction
industries.note: The Infrastructure Renewal Reserve would fund federal highway, public transportation, and Army Corps water construction from offshore royalties and Strategic Petroleum Reserve exchange proceeds. That money only materializes if companies bid on the newly opened leases.

New drilling off the Atlantic coast and within 100-125 miles of Florida would put coastal economies that depend on clean water and beaches at risk from spills and platform construction. These industries and coastal residents lose together under the bill.

industries.industry: Offshore renewable energy and marine aquaculture
industries.note: The bill authorizes commercial lease sales for offshore renewable energy and for cultivating marine organisms, though it bars the offshore resource inventory from restricting oil and gas leasing in any way.
